newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed aide urges Russian economic U-turn.
newsitem.headline: Lebed aide urges Russian economic U-turn.

text.p: A senior economist close to security chief Alexander Lebed said on Thursday that slumping industrial production posed the biggest threat to Russia's national survival and urged a radical change of course.
Sergei Glazyev, who heads the economic section of the powerful Security Council, also criticised the government for failing to pursue policy goals set by President Boris Yeltsin.
"We believe the main threat to national security lies in the continuing economic depression," Glazyev, a former Russian foreign trade minister, told a news conference.
He said a third of Russia's big industrial enterprises were bankrupt and a further third were on the brink of it. The government should cut interest rates to avoid economic collapse.
The government, following recipes from the International Monetary Fund, has deliberately kept monetary policy tight.
Glazyev said Russia's proposed budget for 1997, which aims to keep inflation firmly under control, would deepen the economic malaise and stoke up social tensions.
"For 1997 they have proposed to us zero growth in production that preserves the depression and accelerates the chaos which in turn leads to a shrinking of the national wealth," he said.
Russia's gross domestic product (GDP) and industrial production both contracted by five percent in the first half of 1996 compared with the same period a year earlier.

However, consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in August and the government, helped by a $10 billion three-year IMF loan, hopes to bring the annual figure down to 22 percent this year, from 131 percent in 1995.
"Low inflation is good but that cannot be our sole aim if we want to see economic growth," Glazyev said, noting that high interest rates had exacerbated the government's debts.
He also called for fiscal reforms to stimulate investment and for the creation of development banks to channel funds into industry as in Japan and some other countries.
Glazyev said government decisions diverged from the aims of the president.

"The government (of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin) should work towards the goals of the president. We criticise it on the grounds that their decisions contradict those goals," he said, citing such issues as the non-payment of salaries.
"A most dramatic situation is developing in the armed forces, which need twice as much money as the state budget can afford," he said.
Earlier on Thursday Lebed, an ambitious general who came a strong third in this summer's presidential poll, repeated a warning that the cash-strapped army was close to mutiny.

Lebed, secretary of the Security Council which groups senior ministers, appears to be jostling with Chernomyrdin and other officials for position in the political vacuum that has emerged in Moscow as doctors prepare Yeltsin for heart surgery.
Lebed recently called for an overhaul of the 1997 budget, saying more money should be made available to the armed forces, agriculture, heavy industry and other sectors.
He proposed raising the extra revenues by hiking prices of natural resources, ending preferential import duties for foreign firms and charging higher rents for the use of state property.
Lebed, a controversial figure, is mistrusted by many in the Kremlin, especially after his apparent success in engineering a ceasefire in the breakaway republic of Chechnya.
Glazyev said he would fly to Chechnya on Friday to discuss the economic reconstruction of the war-battered region.

"But we will not be bearing any gifts with us," he added. He said there was no question of compensating people for losses incurred during the war, which he said were the result of an unlawful rebellion against the state.
